title: The gospel
hookLine: everyone stands, three small crosses on forehead, lips and heart

lines: ALLELUIA, AND THE BOOK HELD HIGH.
cards: Alleluia. After sitting through the first readings and the psalm, the whole church is suddenly on its feet, singing that one word over and over. Candles move.
Sometimes incense rises. A deacon or the priest lifts a big, ornate book from the altar and carries it high to the ambo, like a banner.
And when he announces which Gospel he's reading from, the congregation does something small and quick with their thumbs that a visitor can easily miss. Forehead. Lips.

teach.b: Gospel is an old English word: god spel, good news. It translates the Greek euangelion, a word the Roman world used for a herald's announcement, like news of a victory.
Mark's Gospel opens with it, in the Douay-Rheims: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God."
For Catholics, the Gospel reading is the high point of the listening part of the Mass, because here Christ himself speaks, in his own words and deeds. So the body changes.

Everyone stands, the way you'd stand when someone important walks in. Alleluia, a Hebrew word meaning praise the Lord, greets it; in Lent, when the Alleluia goes quiet, another short acclamation takes its place.

teach.h: ONLY A DEACON OR PRIEST READS IT.
teach.b: Only a deacon or a priest reads the Gospel, and before he does, he quietly asks to be made worthy of it. Then he announces it: a reading from the holy Gospel according to Matthew, or Mark, or Luke, or John.

That's when the thumbs move: a small cross on the forehead, on the lips, over the heart. Catholics often explain it as a silent prayer without words: may this word be in my mind, on my lips, and in my heart.
Understand it, say it, love it.

teach.h: THE BEGINNING OF THE GOSPEL OF JESUS CHRIST.
teach.b: When the reading ends, the priest or deacon kisses the page, and quietly says a Latin line asking that through the words of the Gospel, our sins may be wiped away. A book, kissed. News worth standing up for.

how: At Mass the congregation stands for the Gospel, sings the Alleluia (another acclamation in Lent), and traces small crosses on forehead, lips and heart as the deacon or priest announces the reading; he kisses the book at the end.

games.why: three small crosses with the thumb: may this word be in my mind, on my lips and in my heart.

practice: If you're Catholic, or you'd like to try it, trace a small cross with your thumb on your forehead, your lips and your heart: in my mind, on my lips, in my heart.
If you'd rather not, just touch each place lightly, or simply notice it. Then bring back any line of a Gospel you know, and let it sit in all three places.
